caption:
Which of these 7 Edinburgh secrets didn't you know? Comment the number 👇

1. Castle Rock
Edinburgh Castle sits on Castle Rock, the plug of hard volcanic rock left from a volcano that erupted around 340 million years ago. Glaciers later scraped away the softer rock around it, leaving the crag standing tall.

2. Mary King's Close
This cramped Old Town street was partly demolished from 1753 so the Royal Exchange (today's City Chambers) could be built on top. Its lower floors survived underground as the building's foundations, and opened to visitors in 2003.

3. Greyfriars Bobby
As the story goes, after his owner died in 1858, a Skye Terrier named Bobby kept returning to the grave in Greyfriars Kirkyard for 14 years, until his own death in 1872. In 1867 the Lord Provost paid for his dog licence and gave him a collar, now in the Museum of Edinburgh.

4. The One O'Clock Gun
Edinburgh Castle has fired the One O'Clock Gun every day except Sundays, Good Friday and Christmas Day since 1861. It began as a time signal so ships on the Firth of Forth could set their chronometers, even on days too foggy to see the time ball on Calton Hill.

5. Scott Monument
This Gothic spire on Princes Street, finished in the 1840s to honor novelist Sir Walter Scott, rises 61 meters and has 287 steps to the top. It's the second-largest monument to a writer in the world, after the José Martí memorial in Havana.

6. New Town
In 1766, Edinburgh's council ran a competition to plan a new Georgian district beyond the crowded Old Town. The winner was James Craig, a little-known architect in his twenties. His grid of streets and squares is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

7. Edinburgh Festival Fringe
In 1947, eight theater companies turned up uninvited to the first Edinburgh International Festival and put on their own shows in spare venues. That gatecrash became the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, now billed as the world's largest performing arts festival.
